question: Which health workers are most often involved in giving injections and face the highest risk of medication administration errors?
explanation: Nurses administer the majority of parenteral medications, placing them at the forefront of both care delivery and procedural risk. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h1)

question: An unsafe injection primarily puts which two people at risk in a healthcare setting?
explanation: Poor injection practices directly expose the recipient to pathogens while simultaneously endangering the healthcare worker administering the dose. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h1)

question: Which needle-recapping method causes the most accidental needle-stick injuries?
explanation: Using both hands to recap places the guiding hand directly in the path of the sharp point if it misses the sheath. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h2)

question: What happens if a nurse uses a syringe that already touched a patient to draw medicine from a shared multi-dose vial?

options.B: Contamination of the vial for future users
options.C: Complete evaporation of the liquid content
options.D: Immediate neutralization of the drug potency

explanation: Re-using a syringe in a multi-dose vial introduces patient pathogens directly into the shared medicine supply. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h2)

question: Which blood-borne infection has the highest chance of spreading after a single accidental needle-stick injury?
explanation: Hepatitis B has the highest transmission rate among common blood-borne pathogens following percutaneous exposure. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h3)

question: Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) is an urgent medicine given quickly after potential exposure to which virus?
explanation: PEP drugs are prescribed promptly following suspected or confirmed occupational exposure to HIV to prevent infection. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h3)

question: What usually happens in a hospital ward when safety needles and devices are constantly out of stock?

options.A: Immediate closure of the affected facility

explanation: When proper equipment is unavailable, staff often resort to unsafe workarounds to complete required clinical tasks. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h4)

question: Heavy workloads and too few nurses on duty often lead to which problem during medication rounds?
explanation: Severe time constraints push busy practitioners to skip essential infection prevention steps to save time. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h4)

question: What is the single most important action to stop germs from spreading between patients in a hospital?
explanation: Regular and correct handwashing or sanitizing removes transient microorganisms and prevents the spread of pathogens. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h5)

question: Where must a used syringe and needle be thrown immediately after giving an injection?
explanation: Puncture-resistant safety containers placed at the point of use prevent accidental needle pricks and injury. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h6)

question: What is the very first thing you should do if you accidentally prick yourself with a used needle?

options.A: Wrap the finger tightly and finish the shift
options.B: Scrub the wound vigorously with a hard brush
options.C: Apply concentrated bleach to kill surface bacteria
options.D: Wash the site immediately with soap and running water

explanation: Washing the area gently with soap and water minimizes pathogen entry without causing further tissue trauma. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h6)

question: Why is it important for a hospital to have an open, blame-free system for reporting needle-stick injuries?

options.A: It ensures swift disciplinary action for the affected nurse
options.B: It eliminates the need for standard precautions training
options.C: It allows prompt medical evaluation and tracks ward hazards
options.D: It reduces the financial budget required for safety boxes

explanation: A blame-free reporting culture encourages prompt post-exposure care and highlights systemic equipment failures. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a good way to reduce sharp injuries among nursing staff?

options.C: Punishing nurses publicly for every reported incident
options.D: Integrating safety competencies into basic training

explanation: Punitive measures drive injuries underground and discourage staff from reporting exposures or seeking timely prophylaxis. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h7)
